documents.abstract: مفهوم الأرجونوميك (Ergonomics) في تصميم اللوحات التصويرية داخل مباني المستشفيات، وتحليل مردودها النفسي على المرضى والمراجعين والأطباء والاداريين. واهمية الارجنومية في توزيع لوحات التصوير داخل المستشفى تسهم بفاعلية في خلق بيئة علاجية إيجابية، تعزز الإحساس بالراحة والأمان، وتقلل من مشاعر القلق والعزلة، كما تدعم التواصل الإنساني والجمالي داخل فضاءات المستشفيات. اعتمدت الدراسة على المنهج الوصفي التحليلي، من خلال تحليل مجموعة من الاعمال الفنية المطبقة في مستشفيات محلية وعالمية، ودراسة العلاقة بين اللون، والضوء، والموضوع الفني، وتأثيرها على الحالة النفسية للمرضى. وعرض الفن البصري، وخاصة ما يتعلق باللوحات من الطبيعة والاعمال التجريدية وغيرها من الأساليب الفنية، يمكن أن يكون لها آثار إيجابية على النتائج الصحية والاثار الإيجابية على النتائج الصحية، وزيادة التسامح عن الألم وانخفاض القلق لدى المريض. من خلال هذا البحث سوف نتناول الاعتبارات الارجنومية في تصميم اللوحات الجدارية لمباني المستشفيات من خلال التصميم والألوان واهمية الضوء. تهتم الارجنومية بالتوافق بين الانسان والمكونات الأخرى التي تحيط به والمثيرات التي يتعامل ويتفاعل معها فى نظام حياته اليومية سواء من الناحية النفسية او البدنية مما تعود علية بالراحة والأمان النفسي وتخفيف معاناته والضغوط عليه. اللوحات التصويرية تعتبر من الفنون البصرية التي تقوم بدور مهم ووسيط اتصال مع المتلقي في مخاطبة جميع حواسه لتحقيق الراحة النفسية له، والانطباع الذهني الذي تطبعه بالتأثير على قدراته وإدراكه الحسي والمعرفي لتحقيق الراحة والسعادة له.

Die Seite dokumentiert eine preregistrierte Studie, in der dein 5D-Framework und die 25-Item Intrinsic Motivation Profile (IMP) Scale erstmals konfirmatorisch getestet werden, inklusive eines Vergleichs von multiplikativen 5D-Modellen mit klassischen additiven SDT-Modellen zur Vorhersage von Lebenszufriedenheit. Inhaltliche Kernaussage Im Zentrum steht die Idee, intrinsische Motivation als fünfdimensionale Struktur zu modellieren, die mittels konfirmatorischer Faktorenanalyse (CFA) in einer deutschsprachigen Erwachsenstichprobe (N = 400, Prolific) überprüft wird. Die IMP-Skala wird mit der Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS) und der IPIP-NEO-120 Version der Big Five verknüpft, um sowohl Vorhersagekraft für Lebenszufriedenheit als auch konvergente und diskriminante Validität zu testen. Methodisch nutzt die Studie R und das Paket lavaan, mit robusten Schätzverfahren, mehreren Fit-Indizes (CFI, TLI, RMSEA, SRMR) und einem klar festgelegten Plan zum Umgang mit fehlenden Werten. Die zentrale Hypothese H1 prüft, ob ein Fünf-Faktoren-Modell der IMP-Skala gut zu den Daten passt. H2 vergleicht, ob ein multiplikatives Modell der 5D-Faktoren (also Interaktion/Resonanz der Dimensionen) additive SDT-Modelle bei der Vorhersage der SWLS-Werte übertrifft. H3 untersucht, ob die fünf IMP-Faktoren erwartbare Muster mit Big-Five-Dimensionen zeigen, z.B. Zusammenhänge mit Extraversion, Gewissenhaftigkeit und Neurotizismus, ohne in einfache Redundanz zu kippen. Analytische Strategie und Open Science Die CFA dient dazu, die faktorenanalytische Gültigkeit der IMP-Skala zu prüfen, bevor strukturelle Pfadmodelle für Lebenszufriedenheit getestet werden. Für den Vergleich von multiplikativen vs. additiven Modellen werden Informationskriterien und Fit-Indizes herangezogen, um zu entscheiden, welches Modell die SWLS-Daten besser abbildet. Die Validitätsprüfungen basieren auf Korrelationen und Strukturpfaden zwischen IMP-Faktoren und Big Five, mit Fokus auf theoretisch begründeten Mustern statt bloß maximaler Varianzaufklärung. Das Projekt folgt Open-Science-Standards: Preregistration, offene Materialien, geplanter Upload anonymisierter Daten und vollständiger R-Skripte auf OSF. Abweichungen vom ursprünglichen Plan sollen transparent in Projekt-Notizen oder zusätzlichen Registrierungen dokumentiert werden, um nachträgliches „p-Hacking“ und HARKing sichtbar zu machen. Autorischer Kontext Im Author’s Note verortest du dich explizit als radikal ehrlicher, dekonstruktivistischer Autodidakt mit ADHS, der kleine Lügen körperlich nicht toleriert und Systeme als veränderbare Strukturen begreift. Philosophisch beschreibst du ein Denken in verschränkten Systemen zwischen Quantenphysik und Bewusstsein, in dem radikale Eigenverantwortung und Demut koexistieren, inklusive der bewussten Entscheidung, Zukunft nicht kontrollieren zu wollen, um psychisch nicht zu kollabieren. Wissenschaftlich rahmst du das 5D-Framework als Transformationsmodell intrinsischer Motivation, das Neurobiologie, Quantensysteme, Systemtheorie (emergent vs. hierarchisch) und Bildungspsychologie bündelt. Emotional positionierst du das Projekt als Versuch, dein intrinsisch gewachsenes Modell in die Sprache der empirischen Psychologie zu übersetzen, mit expliziter Bereitschaft, dich von Daten korrigieren zu lassen und Menschen zu finden, die deine Klarheit als Einladung statt Angriff erleben. Projektstruktur auf OSF Das OSF-Projekt ist aktuell privat, enthält aber bereits Komponenten für Daten, Dokumentation und Materialien, in denen u.a. ein akademischer Forschungsplan, System-Thesis und ein Text „The 5D-Framework: A Unified Theory of Systemic Resonance“ abgelegt sind. Es existiert ein verlinktes Unterprojekt speziell für die IMP-Validierungsstudie, das ebenfalls als Repository für Preregistration und Daten fungiert. Das Projekt ist thematisch in Psychologie, Sozial- und Verhaltenswissenschaften sowie Quantitative Psychologie einsortiert und nutzt eine CC BY 4.0 Lizenz.

In human-computer collaboration, machines’ limited emotion perception hinders natural interaction. Gait is a promising channel for emotion recognition because it is non-intrusive and available at a distance. Existing end-to-end models often require expert architecture design, large annotated datasets, and offer limited interpretability. To address these issues, we propose a human-computer collaborative modeling method that integrates psychological knowledge with machine learning. Validated cues from psychological research are transformed into structured features, including objective, kinematic, and smoothness features, to provide a theory-guided, information-rich input space. Based on this strategy, we develop a Psychology-Informed Random Forest model for gait-emotion prediction. Experiments with ten-fold cross-validation on the Emotion-Gait dataset show that the model achieves 83.69% accuracy, outperforming the closest baseline by 1.54%. The findings demonstrate that psychology-guided feature design can improve both prediction performance and interpretability in affective interaction research.

Abstract The development of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools capable of producing wholly or partially synthetic child sexual abuse material (AI CSAM) presents profound challenges for child protection, law enforcement, and societal responses to child exploitation. While some argue that the harmfulness of AI CSAM differs fundamentally from other CSAM due to a perceived absence of direct victimization, this perspective fails to account for the range of risks associated with its production and consumption. AI has been implicated in the creation of synthetic CSAM of children who have not previously been abused, the revictimization of known survivors of abuse, the facilitation of grooming, coercion, and sexual extortion, and the normalization of child sexual exploitation. Additionally, AI CSAM may serve as a new or enhanced pathway into offending by lowering barriers to engagement, desensitizing users to progressively extreme content, and undermining protective factors for individuals with a sexual interest in children. Drawing on a narrative review and conceptual synthesis of technical literature, psychological and criminological research, and civil society and law enforcement reporting, this paper provides a high-level primer on key generative AI technologies and examines the harms associated with AI CSAM. It cautions against claims that AI CSAM may function as a harm reduction tool, emphasizing how appeals to harmlessness obscure real risks and may contribute to inertia in ecosystem responses.

Teleoperation refers to the control of robotic systems that extend an operator’s perceptual and manipulative capabilities in remote environments. Prior studies have identified the individual effects of control frame and view on teleoperation performance, yet their interaction remains insufficiently examined. This study investigates how different control frames and views, both individually and jointly, affect directional judgment during the control of a remote robot arm’s movements using a handheld controller. Experimental results based on objective measures including task performance and eye tracking show that reaction time and error rates decrease when the spatial information required by the control frame is consistent with the visual cues provided by the view. Subjective usability evaluations further indicate a preference for control frames that minimize mental transformation and views offering a broader field of view. These findings highlight the importance of aligning control and view representations to improve performance and usability in teleoperation systems.

Hollnagel’s work on Safety-I and Safety-II, Work-as-Imagined (WAI) and Work-as-Done (WAD), and the Efficiency–Thoroughness Trade-Off (ETTO) has reshaped how safety researchers and practitioners understand human performance in complex systems. Building on this legacy, the present study investigates how workers in a petrochemical facility navigate written procedures during everyday operations. Using head-mounted video recordings, we analyzed 1,422 procedural steps across 40 operations, comparing paper-based and digital procedures. A Skip-Order-Action (SOA) Framework is introduced to investigate deviations between WAI and WAD, moving beyond binary notions of compliance and non-compliance. Results showed that approximately one-third of steps deviated from prescribed methods, yet all tasks were completed successfully, underscoring the adaptive role of procedural variation. Analyses further revealed that the type of procedural variation (Skip, Order, Action) changed significantly depending on the operational phase. Crucially, variability was driven primarily by contextual factors, such as operational phase and procedural medium, rather than individual worker differences, emphasizing the systemic nature of adaptation. These findings provide empirical support for Hollnagel’s call to understand why work succeeds and demonstrate how procedural variability can be conceptualized as functional adaptation rather than error. By operationalizing Safety-II concepts through the SOA Framework, this study extends Hollnagel’s vision of safety as an emergent property of everyday work.

In a world where the pursuit of happiness is often reduced to fleeting pleasures, Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA., presents a thought-provoking exploration of what it truly means to attain deep and enduring fulfillment. Published in 2002 by The United Nations and The Education Training Centre, this book challenges the modern obsession with immediate gratification and introduces a philosophical framework that transcends transient joys. Drawing upon ancient wisdom and contemporary insights, the author navigates the complexities of human desires, ethical considerations, and the fundamental principles that contribute to a life of meaning. Through a meticulous blend of philosophical analysis and real-world applications, this book invites readers to rethink their definitions of happiness and consider how they can cultivate a richer, more fulfilling existence beyond the confines of pleasure alone. The foundation of this book is rooted in a critical analysis of why contemporary societies often equate happiness with momentary pleasure. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA. examines how historical perspectives on fulfillment have evolved and how modern interpretations sometimes deviate from the deeper philosophical insights of the past. This book was published in 2002 at The United Nations and The Education Training Centre as an academic yet accessible contribution to the discourse on happiness and ethical living. To establish a well-rounded exploration, the book defines key concepts such as pleasure, fulfillment, virtue, and contentment. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA. dissects these ideas from multiple philosophical traditions, contrasting hedonistic pursuits with more sustainable forms of well-being that integrate personal growth, moral responsibility, and intellectual development. Phenomena that prompted this book’s creation include the increasing prevalence of consumerism, the growing dissatisfaction in wealthier societies despite economic prosperity, and the rise of mental health concerns related to the relentless chase of short-term pleasures. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA. highlights how these issues underscore the necessity of a paradigm shift in how fulfillment is conceptualized and pursued. At the core of this book lies an in-depth analysis of ethical principles that guide individuals toward meaningful living. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA. articulates how moral integrity, self-awareness, and purposeful action serve as fundamental pillars of lasting fulfillment. This section presents philosophical models that aid individuals in evaluating their own lives and making conscious choices that align with deeper values rather than transient desires. The book identifies measurable indicators that help readers assess whether their lives are oriented toward true fulfillment. These indicators include emotional stability, resilience in adversity, intrinsic motivation, and the ability to derive satisfaction from meaningful contributions rather than materialistic accumulation. To operationalize these philosophical insights, Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA. introduces a set of practical methodologies that allow readers to apply abstract concepts in their daily lives. These include mindfulness practices, ethical decision-making frameworks, and strategies to develop emotional intelligence and interpersonal relationships. Several factors influence the pursuit of lasting fulfillment, ranging from cultural expectations to individual psychological conditioning. This section dissects external and internal elements that either facilitate or hinder a person’s journey toward deeper satisfaction, emphasizing the role of self-discipline, societal values, and education. Practical implementation strategies involve structured approaches that integrate philosophical understanding into daily life. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA. proposes actionable steps for individuals, educators, and policymakers to foster environments that encourage sustainable happiness rather than short-lived pleasures. No philosophical inquiry is without its challenges. This book addresses both the obstacles and supporting elements in the quest for fulfillment, including societal pressures, misconceptions about happiness, and the difficulty of shifting ingrained habits. At the same time, it presents avenues for support, such as philosophical communities, ethical education, and personal introspection. The conclusion synthesizes key arguments, reinforcing the necessity of transitioning from pleasure-driven pursuits to a more profound engagement with life’s purpose. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA. leaves readers with a reflective framework to continue their philosophical journey toward authentic and enduring fulfillment.

This study investigates how demographic homophily between audiences and virtual influencers (VIs) shapes the effectiveness of pro-environmental campaigns. A between-subjects online experiment employing a 2 (age homophily: outgroup vs. ingroup) × 2 (racial homophily: outgroup vs. ingroup) × 2 (gender homophily: outgroup vs. ingroup) factorial design was conducted with 430 U.S. social media users, who were exposed to simulated Instagram posts featuring VIs promoting an eyewear brand’s sustainability initiative. Grounded in Social Identity Theory, the findings reveal that age, race, and gender homophily exert both direct and interactive effects on attitudes toward VIs and green behavioral intentions, with the strongest responses emerging when all dimensions align. Moreover, wishful identification fully mediated the effects of homophily on both outcomes, while perceived similarity influenced only green behavioral intention. The study extends identity-based perspectives to virtual communication and provides actionable insights for practitioners seeking to strategically leverage VIs in social marketing campaigns.

ObjectiveThis study comparatively evaluated three assembly manual types (traditional paper-based, user-fixed AR, and world-fixed AR) in terms of task performance, dlPFC hemodynamic responses, and perceived workload.BackgroundPrior studies of AR and traditional assembly manuals have relied mainly on subjective workload ratings, providing only an indirect view of cognitive effort. Neurophysiological assessment can quantify mental workload more directly. Measuring dlPFC activation may offer a process-specific index of cognitive control demands.MethodTwenty-four participants performed a 7-min modified Purdue Pegboard Test with each manual type in a within-subjects design. Task performance, dlPFC hemodynamic responses, and perceived workload were assessed. fNIRS was used to measure hemodynamic responses.ResultsThe world-fixed AR manual yielded significantly better task performance than both paper-based and user-fixed AR manuals, particularly in reducing location errors. Both AR manuals elicited significantly higher dlPFC activation than the paper-based manual, indicating elevated cognitive control demands. Perceived workload did not differ significantly across manual types.ConclusionThe world-fixed AR manual improved task performance by reducing information access cost, yet both AR manuals increased cognitive control demands relative to the paper-based manual, likely due to perceptual conflicts inherent in AR. The user-fixed AR manual did not outperform the paper-based version, indicating that AR effectiveness depends on design specifics.ApplicationThe study recommends the world-fixed AR manual among the three types examined while emphasizing the need for innovations that reduce perceptual conflicts. It also shows that neurophysiological assessment provides insights beyond task performance and subjective ratings, supporting multidimensional evaluation to optimize interface technologies.

Context: Strategic corporate training is essential for the sustained professional development of software engineers. However, there is a knowledge gap regarding the factors that drive quality and effectiveness of such training from the professionals' perspective, and no validated instrument exists for assessing these factors in the software engineering (SE) domain. Objective: This study aims to quantitatively analyze which factors influence SE professionals' perceptions of corporate training quality and effectiveness. Method: A quantitative survey was conducted with 282 Brazilian SE professionals. A structured questionnaire was developed and polychoric correlation was adopted for data analysis. Results: Three tightly correlated factors (cognitive engagement, variety of activities, and instructor performance) emerged as the strongest predictors of perceived training quality and effectiveness. Mandatory participation significantly reduces motivation and perceived training quality. Perceived impact on personal time proved to be largely independent of training quality. These findings are consistent with the general training effectiveness literature. Conclusions: Training effectiveness in the SE context is predominantly determined by three factors: cognitive engagement, variety of activities, and instructor performance. Mandatory participation negatively influences motivation, perceived relevance, and perceived training quality, while also amplifying the perception of time burden. The consistency with the general literature suggests that software organizations do not need to reinvent training design principles and can apply established guidelines with confidence. Salas and Cannon-Bowers' framework produced coherent results in the SE context, making it a promising candidate for future psychometric validation.

documents.abstract: Digital humans are lifelike virtual agents capable of natural conversation and are increasingly deployed in domains like retail and finance. However, most current digital humans operate in isolation from their surroundings and lack contextual awareness beyond the dialogue itself. We address this limitation by integrating ambient intelligence (AmI) - i.e., environmental sensors, IoT data, and contextual modeling - with digital human systems. This integration enables situational awareness of the user's environment, anticipatory and proactive assistance, seamless cross-device interactions, and personalized long-term user support. We present a conceptual framework defining key roles that AmI can play in shaping digital human behavior, a design space highlighting dimensions such as proactivity levels and privacy strategies, and application-driven patterns with case studies in financial and retail services. We also discuss an architecture for ambient-enabled digital humans and provide guidelines for responsible design regarding privacy and data governance. Together, our work positions ambient intelligent digital humans as a new class of interactive agents powered by AI that respond not only to users' queries but also to the context and situations in which the interaction occurs.

documents.abstract: In recent years, the gap between the rich and the poor has widened, and polarization of public opinion has been observed worldwide. Is there a possibility that such disparity will lead to the fixation of awareness for economic status? If so, how would the difference be identified through text analysis? This study used text analysis of post-game reports of participants in a Simulated International Society Game, a participatory social simulation taking all day long, to explore the differences in consciousness between groups assigned to the wealthy and those assigned to the poor. The participants were 158 first-year students at Hokkaido University. Participants who had never met each other before were randomly assigned to regions of varying affluence to conduct transactions and to create a virtual society. The game was repeated six times for a 1-h session, assumed to be 1 year. After the game, participants submitted a report describing the events during each session. The latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) topic model was used to analyze these reports. This study investigated how participants assigned to wealthy and poor regions interpreted their experiences in sessions 1–6. The analysis results indicated that participants from the wealthy and poor areas were more likely to refer to different topics. The results suggest that this 1-day experience could make a difference in the consciousness of participants in the wealthy or poor class. The validity of analyzing topic ratios as individual variables was also discussed.

documents.abstract: This study examined the ergonomic effects of HMI design variables determining the manipulation method of dial-type gearshifts. Eight design alternatives were derived by combining two implementation levels for each of three design variables: P-position engagement method (Rotation, Push), Gear indicator location (Up, Left), and Gear position sequence (RND, DNR). Forty-three participants performed gear-shifting tasks using working prototypes of the design alternatives, during which task completion time, number of extra manipulations, perceived workload, perceived safety, and preference were measured. The results revealed the superiority of 1) Push over Rotation; 2) Up over Left under RND, and Left over Up under DNR; 3) RND over DNR in general, and DNR over RND under Left; and 4) combinations of Push-Up-RND and Push-Left-DNR over other design alternatives. The findings and identified ergonomic design characteristics may inform future gearshift HMI designs that prevent driver confusion/misoperation, thereby enhancing driving performance and safety.

Procedural-Practical (P-P) tasks supported by mixed reality (MR) technologies require hand interactions for both virtual and real-world elements, causing workflow disruptions. Previous research has explored lower-limb interactions as a complement to hand-based interactions. However, the optimal design and potential benefits of lower-limb interaction for MR-assisted P-P tasks remain unexplored. To address this, we conducted a two-stage study: (1) an elicitation study generating two lower-limb interaction paradigms and (2) a comprehensive evaluation comparing these two paradigms against each other and against the conventional hand-based paradigm. Our findings reveal that lower-limb interaction paradigms using multi-function foot gestures outperform both single-function foot gestures and conventional hand-based paradigms across most tasks and factors, while conventional interactions remain comparable efficacy for precise tasks like 3D transformations. This research introduces a novel and empirically validated lower-limb interaction paradigm for MR-assisted P-P tasks, offering insights into leveraging lower-limb interactions to enhance experiences and efficiency in MR-assisted P-P tasks.

documents.abstract: Stroke and other disorders resulting in vestibular dysfunction are a leading cause of balance impairment and functional disability in adults, both in the United States and worldwide. In the United States, roughly 795,000 people a year experience a stroke, the majority of which are 65 and older (Martin et al., 2025). In that demographic, stroke reduces mobility in more than half of survivors, and much of this mobility loss attributable to balance deficits (Feigin et al., 2025). Globally, there are roughly 93.8 million patients who have suffered a stroke, with an annual global incidence rate of approximately 11.9 million. Conservatively, roughly 20% of those who have suffered a stroke report balance impairment, but individual studies report rates as high as 83% (CDC). Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo is estimated to impact roughly 2.4% of the population over the course of our lifetimes. Among adults over 60, the prevalence rises to about 3.5%, and cumulative lifetime incidence by 80 years old is roughly 10% (Lindell et al., 2024). Conventional rehabilitation programs have persistently faced challenges with patient engagement and adherence (Shahhar et al., 2022). Gamification and VR-based rehabilitation leverage principles of motor learning, neuroplasticity, and intrinsic motivation to address these limitations.

Contemporary intelligent systems increasingly participate in shaping, rather than merely supporting, human decision-making processes. While these systems enhance efficiency and predictive performance, they also introduce a critical but underexamined challenge: decisions may remain technically valid while becoming difficult for human actors to interpret and internalize. This misalignment is conceptualized in this study as the meaning gap, defined as the divergence between system output and human interpretive understanding.This paper proposes a human-centered governance framework that positions cognitive sovereignty—the capacity of individuals and institutions to interpret, contextualize, and assume responsibility for decisions—as a necessary condition for sustainable sociotechnical systems. The framework is structured around ten interdependent principles that collectively redefine governance as a cognitive architecture embedded within system design.Drawing on interdisciplinary literature in human–AI interaction, interpretability, and decision science, the study introduces latency as a conceptual construct describing temporal misalignment between system output and human interpretive readiness. This construct provides an integrative lens for understanding phenomena such as delayed comprehension, reduced accountability, and unstable trust in algorithmically mediated environments.Rather than treating interpretability as an auxiliary feature, the proposed framework positions it as a core system function. The paper further outlines potential pathways for operationalizing the meaning gap through measurable indicators, including time-to-comprehension, decision override frequency, and confidence misalignment.While existing frameworks have called for interpretability, few have proposed measurable indicators of cognitive alignment. This paper contributes preliminary metrics—time-to-comprehension, decision override frequency, and confidence misalignment—that operationalize the meaning gap for empirical testing.

documents.abstract: Police officers are repeatedly exposed to critical incidents, making them vulnerable to posttraumatic stress symptoms (PTSS) during service and posttraumatic stress disorder. Trauma-related coping self-efficacy (CSE) has been identified as a protective factor in posttraumatic recovery, yet little is known about its role in high-risk occupations. This study integrates the CSE framework into the cumulative burden model and examines longitudinal associations of CSE and accumulated critical incident history (CIH) with PTSS 1 year later in 2,954 police officers, while adjusting for multiple individual and organizational risk factors. The study also examines whether CIH modifies the CSE-PTSS association. Results showed that CSE was inversely associated, and CIH positively associated, with later PTSS. A small yet significant CIH × CSE interaction was found and stratified analyses indicated stronger CSE-PTSS associations at higher levels of CIH. Notably, post hoc analyses also showed lower mean CSE among officers with the highest CIH, indicating a potentially concerning pattern between cumulative exposure and strained CSE beliefs. The study provides novel etiological insights into the interplay of CSE as a protective factor and CIH as an occupational risk, underscoring their value in organizational prevention. Given the modest effect size, the interaction warrants cautious interpretation, although main findings remained consistent across sensitivity analyses, including models accounting for exposure during the 1-year follow up. Future research is needed to clarify the mechanisms linking critical incident exposure, CSE, and PTSS, and to identify factors that strengthen CSE in policing and other high-risk occupations. Data communication entails ethical dilemmas where situational constraints forbid full disclosure of source data. Whereas visualization research and pedagogy often frames ethics as a matter of individuals making deceptive design choices or being misled, disclosure problems involve negotiation between pro-social actors. To provide observability into these situated judgments, we contribute Purrsuasion, an open-source visualization game where participants play the roles of (i) data providers designing visualizations subject to disclosure constraints and (ii) data seekers requesting information and awarding a contract. We deploy Purrsuasion in an undergraduate data science class (N = 27), gathering gameplay data to support a mixed-methods analysis of students' communication dynamics, problem solving, and trust formation. We find that difficulties envisioning an ideal visualization solution lead to satisficing in visualization authoring and difficulties attributing authorial intent. Given these challenges, we approach scoring student solutions by developing a heuristic rubric that supports sociotechnical judgments of disclosure adherence.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for analytical tasks, yet their effectiveness in real-world applications remains underexamined, partly due to the opacity of proprietary models. We evaluate ChatGPT (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4) on the practical task of extracting research challenges from a large scholarly corpus in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI). Using a two-step approach, we first apply GPT-3.5 to extract candidate challenges from the 879 papers in the 2023 ACM CHI Conference proceedings, then use GPT-4 to select the most relevant challenges per paper. This process yielded 4,392 research challenges across 113 topics, which we organized through topic modeling and present in an interactive visualization. We compare the identified challenges with previously established HCI grand challenges and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, finding both strong alignment in areas such as ethics and accessibility, and gaps in areas such as human-AI collaboration. A task-specific evaluation with human raters confirmed near-perfect agreement that the extracted statements represent plausible research challenges (κ = 0.97). The two-step approach proved cost-effective at approximately US$50 for the full corpus, suggesting that LLMs offer a practical means for qualitative text analysis at scale, particularly for prototyping research ideas and examining corpora from multiple analytical perspectives.

documents.abstract: Altruism, a timeless virtue that transcends cultural boundaries, is the essence of selfless giving and the foundation of genuine human connection. This book by Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, explores the intricate relationship between altruistic behavior and the fulfillment of human potential. Published in 2002 by The United Nations and The Education Training Centre, it delves into the ethical and philosophical dimensions of generosity, unraveling how the act of giving contributes to an enriched, more meaningful existence. Through a comprehensive phenomenological approach, this work highlights the profound joy derived from altruism, arguing that the true essence of happiness is deeply rooted in the well-being of others. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, presents a thought-provoking analysis of the intrinsic motivations behind altruism, examining how societies have historically understood and embraced the act of giving. The book was published in 2002 as a response to the growing interest in ethical philosophy, psychological well-being, and global humanitarian efforts. Drawing from a rich tapestry of philosophical traditions and empirical studies, it addresses the fundamental question of whether giving is an obligation, a virtue, or a natural inclination of human beings. Altruism, as defined by Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, is an intentional action performed for the benefit of others without expecting a return. This book distinguishes between various forms of altruism, from reciprocal kindness to absolute selflessness. The text further explores how altruism is shaped by social, moral, and psychological frameworks, making it both an individual and collective phenomenon. In an era characterized by increasing individualism, Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, investigates why acts of generosity continue to persist. The book presents an exploration of historical and contemporary examples of altruistic behavior, examining how human societies have cultivated cultures of giving. By analyzing these patterns, it uncovers the ways in which altruism influences social cohesion, mental well-being, and ethical consciousness. This book outlines the essential mechanisms through which altruism functions in daily life. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, examines the cognitive and emotional drivers behind selfless acts, demonstrating that the motivation to give stems from a combination of moral philosophy, neurological responses, and socio-cultural conditioning. A critical aspect of this discussion is identifying the markers of altruistic behavior. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, presents a framework for assessing altruism, including psychological traits, behavioral patterns, and societal impact. These indicators provide insight into how selflessness manifests across different contexts. The book investigates variables that influence altruistic tendencies, from genetic predispositions to environmental conditions. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, evaluates how economic status, education, and cultural values shape an individual’s propensity to give, ultimately arguing that altruism is a complex interplay of intrinsic and extrinsic factors. Building on theoretical foundations, this book proposes practical strategies for cultivating altruism at individual and societal levels. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, introduces educational approaches, policy recommendations, and community-driven initiatives that encourage acts of generosity and ethical responsibility. While altruism is celebrated as a moral ideal, it is not without obstacles. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, explores the psychological and societal barriers that hinder the natural inclination to give, such as self-interest, economic limitations, and cultural biases. At the same time, the book highlights key factors that nurture altruistic behavior, including moral education, positive reinforcement, and institutional support. Bringing together the philosophical, ethical, and psychological dimensions of altruism, Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, concludes that selflessness is not merely an ethical choice but an essential component of human flourishing. The joy of giving is not only a reflection of compassion but a gateway to enduring happiness and personal growth.

This study examines how individual creative producers navigate conflicting valuation standards when multiple audience types are copresent. Drawing on a multiyear participant-observation study of stand-up comedy in Los Angeles, I introduce practical annealing as a real-time, cue-driven competency through which performers reconcile heterogeneous standards across casual consumers, peers, and gatekeepers. Practical annealing unfolds through three situated practices: audience profiling (inferring likely sensibilities from contextual and interactional cues), audience orchestration (forging a workable collective from disparate evaluators), and audience triangulation (surfacing overlaps and selectively prioritizing standards to guide performance choices). I show that the latitude to anneal is not uniform. Permission structures rooted in demographic prototyping and status expand or restrict what moves are legible and sanctionable. Although enacted within moments on stage, repeated reconciliations aggregate into career orientations—toward broad malleability or niche grounding—with implications for bookings, visibility, and market position. Conceptually, the paper shifts attention from evaluators to the subjects of evaluation, specifying real-time practices for managing evaluative plurality under copresence and distinguishing it from sequential experimentation or improvisation. The framework clarifies when and for whom real-time reconciliation is feasible and how microinteractional skill scales into durable trajectories in cultural production and other audience-dependent work.

Prior work showed that a three-step serial implementation of the two-point visual steering model in ACT-R can predict the upper bound of human path-keeping performance, but it is unknown whether the cognitive architecture or the number of processing steps drives this ability. This study compares four implementations: no cognitive architecture, ACT-R, and two variants of QN-MHP, each parameterised to minimise average path-keeping error without fitting to human data. Validation against humans reveals that implementations lacking a cognitive architecture or separate processing of the two visual points exceed human performance, failing to predict realistic upper bounds. Two-step serial processing within a cognitive architecture is necessary and sufficient to retain the predictive capabilities for an upper bound of human steering performance.

Evaluation of robotic manipulation systems has largely relied on fixed benchmarks authored by a small number of experts, where task instances, constraints, and success criteria are predefined and difficult to extend. This paradigm limits who can shape evaluation and obscures how policies respond to user-authored variations in task intent, constraints, and notions of success. We argue that evaluating modern manipulation policies requires reframing evaluation as a language-driven process over structured physical domains. We present RoboPlayground, a framework that enables users to author executable manipulation tasks using natural language within a structured physical domain. Natural language instructions are compiled into reproducible task specifications with explicit asset definitions, initialization distributions, and success predicates. Each instruction defines a structured family of related tasks, enabling controlled semantic and behavioral variation while preserving executability and comparability. We instantiate RoboPlayground in a structured block manipulation domain and evaluate it along three axes. A user study shows that the language-driven interface is easier to use and imposes lower cognitive workload than programming-based and code-assist baselines. Evaluating learned policies on language-defined task families reveals generalization failures that are not apparent under fixed benchmark evaluations. Finally, we show that task diversity scales with contributor diversity rather than task count alone, enabling evaluation spaces to grow continuously through crowd-authored contributions. Background: Generative AI (GenAI) mental health chatbots are increasingly being developed to help address persistent barriers to mental healthcare. Unlike earlier rule-based and retrieval-based systems, GenAI chatbots generate open-ended outputs that can be inaccurate and unsafe. Documented harms from general-purpose GenAI chatbots have highlighted the need for purpose-built interventions with dedicated safeguards, yet how safety is implemented in such interventions remains poorly understood. Methods: This scoping review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, with a prospectively registered and peer-reviewed protocol. A systematic search of seven academic databases and search engines including MEDLINE, Scopus, PsycINFO, ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, Google Scholar and Consensus was conducted in July 2025. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data. Safety mechanisms and risk mitigation strategies were narratively synthesised across three pre-specified domains: technical safeguards, pre-deployment safety considerations, and delivery-phase risk mitigation strategies. Results: Twenty-one studies across 11 countries were included. Most interventions incorporated at least one technical safety mechanism, most commonly fine-tuning and prompt engineering. A smaller subset implemented layered safety architectures combining retrieval systems, content filters or risk classifiers, and rule-based algorithms. Pre-deployment safeguards included clinical expert and user co-design approaches, research ethics procedures, and data privacy measures. During intervention delivery, detailed onboarding with role clarification was common, but human oversight was limited. Crisis referral protocols varied in rigor but were mostly underdeveloped, and systematic adverse event monitoring was sparse. Documented safety failures included missed suicidal ideation and provision of inaccurate clinical information. Conclusion: GenAI chatbot interventions require a robust sociotechnical approach that integrates technical safeguards with user co-design, procedural controls, and human oversight. Future research is needed to evaluate efficacy, improve safeguards, and standardize safety outcome measurement. Regulatory oversight proportional to the risks these systems carry is required to enable integration into stepped or blended mental healthcare.

In recent decades, many organizations have been restructuring in ways that formally decentralize the necessary resources, information, and sociopolitical support, which is labeled "structural empowerment." Although prior research suggests that structural empowerment enhances resource exchanges, I challenge this conventional wisdom by theorizing its potential drawbacks for resource sharing. Integrating the evolutionary perspective of work design and the dominance-prestige model, I developed a comprehensive model of how and when structural empowerment can hinder employees' resource sharing via psychological entitlement. I employed multiwave (Study 1) and multisource (Studies 2 and 3) field surveys and experimental methodology (Study 4) to test my hypotheses. The results reveal that dominance-oriented individuals are more likely to feel entitled in response to structural empowerment. Moreover, psychological entitlement decreases resource sharing. The success of a Blockchain venture critically hinges on the contribution of blockchain developers. Blockchain ventures are typically developed as open-source projects, where some developers contribute voluntarily, while others are motivated by token rewards as an incentive to participate. However, it remains unclear whether tokens can serve as a sustainable and effective incentive in the current volatile cryptocurrency market, where opportunistic activities are prevalent. To address this question, we leverage a unique setting where token incentives are substantially affected during Pump-and-dump events (PD). We examine how developers react to this impact and its potential influence on the blockchain development community. Utilizing the most granular code-development level data from GitHub, we construct two metrics to gauge developer contribution: contribution quantity and originality. We estimate the effect of token incentive on contribution through the interactive fixed effects counterfactual (IFEct) model. The results imply that developers contribute less frequently with lower code originality to the projects due to token value distortion after a PD event. Moreover, we identify the moderation effect of varying degrees of decentralization. The findings suggest that a decreased degree of decentralization can amplify the negative effect of PD, leading to the "Tragedy of the Commons", thereby further diminishing developers’ motivation to contribute. Our research provides important insights into the effectiveness of token incentives in blockchain ventures, underscoring the need for a more sustainable and effective incentive system.

Virtual reality (VR) is emerging as a popular tool for training, but its true efficacy remains unclear. One concern is that differences in sensory input between VR and real-world environments may impact visuomotor learning and transfer. This study focuses on the impact of VR-based training on head movements. Forty-three participants were trained on a reaching task in either a virtual or equivalent physical environment. Head yaw movements were analyzed using kinematic measures including rotation amplitude, duration, and peak acceleration. Participants in the VR-training group produced yaw rotations that were, from the outset, longer in duration and lower in peak acceleration. Their movements also gradually became measurably larger in amplitude. Crucially, VR-trained participants initially exhibited larger yaw amplitudes and rotation durations upon transferring to the real-world task. Hence, learning in VR can promote altered head-movement strategies that temporarily persist after transfer, a finding to consider when designing VR-based training protocols.

Although gender quotas are gaining increasing popularity, evidence on their effectiveness is mixed. While some studies set in Western contexts suggest a positive impact on women's board representation, others demonstrate backlash. Further, because this research primarily treats women as a singular, homogenous group, it overlooks critical intersectionality issues on boards, limiting our understanding of how quotas may shape the outcomes of women directors from marginalized groups. We contribute to this growing scholarly debate on quota effectiveness by examining the outcomes of women directors from both dominant and marginalized groups. Drawing on the instrumental perspective on legitimacy and intersectionality research, we propose that although all women directors gain additional board appointments compared to men when quotas are implemented, marginalized women experience intersectional disadvantages that result in their lower appointment rates compared to dominant women. Importantly, we show that prior executive or independent director experience acts as a powerful equalizer, enabling marginalized women directors to overcome these barriers and close their opportunity gap. We test our hypotheses in the context of India's gender quota policy using archival data on all men and women directors from dominant and marginalized groups (i.e., gender and religion or caste) serving on the boards of the National Stock Exchange (NSE)1500-listed firms from 2013 to 2017 and shed light on the underlying mechanisms using qualitative insights from 37 interviews with directors. Our mixed-methods field data capture real-world board dynamics and maximize ecological validity to provide critical policy implications. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), exemplified by large language models (LLMs), is rapidly approaching and in some cases surpassing human performance across a wide range of cognitive tasks. However, human nature is not limited to intelligence alone; it also encompasses sensibility, including the capacity to perceive and experience beauty in visual scenes. This raises a fundamental question: how humans and AI systems converge or diverge in such aesthetic experiences. Aesthetic evaluation depends not only on objective properties of images but also on internal processes within the observer. As part of ongoing efforts in AI alignment, building upon prior human studies that have examined the relationship between beauty ratings, bodily sensations, and emotions, we adopt a comparable set of questionnaire items and present them to LLMs, enabling a direct comparison between human and AI responses. Our comparative analyses revealed that, while humans and AI exhibited broadly similar patterns in the correlations between beauty ratings and emotions, as well as in the image features they prioritized, notable divergences emerged in both the distribution of emotional responses and the relationship between beauty ratings and bodily sensations. These findings suggest that state-of-the-art LLMs, trained on large-scale textual data, can approximate average human tendencies in aesthetic evaluation to a certain extent. However, they also indicate limitations, particularly in relation to interoceptive aspects, which may reflect insufficient representation in training data or unintended consequences of alignment processes. These findings highlight key challenges for AI alignment and suggest important directions for developing AI systems with human-like aesthetic processing.

AbstractIn the modern globalised world, occupational safety and health (OSH) is increasingly influenced by supply chain requirements and practices, such as certifications and audits. Yet, safety research is mainly aimed at OSH certifications, e.g. ISO 45001, while little attention is paid to other voluntary certification standards or supply chain practices, i.e. buyers’ audits that seek to influence suppliers’ operations, including OSH. This paper examines how a large retailer and its small fruit and vegetable suppliers navigate supply chain requirements and how these affect the suppliers’ OSH management. The analysis reveals that supply chain certifications and the subsequent audits have a positive impact on OSH management and allow small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to make a systematic assessment of their OSH management. Nevertheless, the quality of audits varies, and buyers cannot depend solely on audits to secure compliance with Codes of Conduct (CoC). Furthermore, buyers risk a decoupling between their procurement and CSR departments.

documents.abstract: Maintaining situational awareness in high-stakes multi-robot applications requires balancing exploration of unobserved regions with sustained monitoring of changing Regions of Interest (ROIs), often under unknown and time-varying distributions, partial observability, and limited communication. We propose a decentralized multi-agent coverage framework that serves as a high-level planning strategy, in which each agent computes an adaptive ergodic policy, implemented via a Markov-chain, that tracks an updated belief over the underlying importance map. Beliefs are maintained online via Gaussian Process (GP) regression from local noisy observations exchanged with neighbors. The resulting policy drives agents to spend time in ROIs in proportion to their estimated importance, while preserving sufficient exploration to detect and adapt to time-varying environmental changes. Unlike existing approaches that assume known importance maps, centralized coordination, or a static environment, our framework addresses the combined challenges of unknown, time-varying distributions under a decentralized, partially observable setting. We further show that our framework is robust to communication and memory degradation, robot loss, and can scale up to hundreds of robots.

From Self to Others: A Motivational Theory of Intrapersonal and Interpersonal Growth delves into the intricate relationship between personal motivation and social development. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad presents a compelling theory that connects the drive within an individual to understand and improve themselves (intrapersonal growth) with the equally important journey of building meaningful connections and influence in their social world (interpersonal growth). The book highlights how motivation acts as the essential catalyst bridging self-awareness with empathy, collaboration, and social engagement. This work articulates how nurturing motivation within the self creates pathways to authentic relationships, effective communication, and social harmony. By weaving together psychological insights and practical applications, Rachmad offers a framework that empowers readers to cultivate balanced growth for personal fulfillment and collective wellbeing. Published by UNICEF, this book underscores the universal relevance of harmonizing inner and outer development to foster resilient and compassionate communities. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad authored this book in 1996 as a response to the growing need for a unified understanding of how personal motivation influences social behaviors and vice versa. Recognizing the fragmentation in traditional motivational theories that focused narrowly on individual or social aspects, Rachmad sought to establish a comprehensive theory integrating both domains. The collaboration with UNICEF supported this vision, emphasizing global human development that values both personal insight and interpersonal relations. At its core, this theory distinguishes between intrapersonal growth—the deepening of self-understanding, emotional regulation, and self-motivation—and interpersonal growth—the development of empathy, communication skills, and social connectedness. Motivation is positioned as the dynamic force that activates and sustains growth in both spheres, creating a fluid movement from self-awareness toward meaningful social interaction. This theory emerged from observing how individuals with strong motivational foundations experience enhanced self-esteem and simultaneously engage more positively with others. Conversely, lack of motivation often impairs both self-improvement and social engagement. Societal complexities and rapid interpersonal demands further accentuate the necessity of this integrated motivational perspective. The motivational drive is both intrinsic and relational. Intrinsic motivation fuels personal insight and goal-setting, while relational motivation encourages social bonding and mutual support. These two aspects interact, enabling a cyclical growth pattern that reinforces both self and others’ development. Indicators include sustained self-reflection, purposeful goal pursuit, active listening, empathy in social exchanges, and constructive conflict resolution. Progress in these areas reflects the harmony between intrapersonal and interpersonal motivation. This framework operationalizes variables such as self-motivation intensity, emotional awareness, social engagement frequency, communication quality, and relational satisfaction. Measurement of these variables utilizes psychological scales, behavioral observations, and qualitative assessments. Factors that determine growth include individual personality traits, cultural values, environmental support, educational opportunities, and quality of social relationships. Rachmad stresses the importance of nurturing environments that cultivate both personal ambition and social responsibility. Effective implementation involves educational programs that blend self-awareness exercises with social skills training, community-building activities, mentorship, and reflective practices. UNICEF’s global outreach facilitates the adoption of these strategies in diverse cultural contexts. Challenges include cultural stigmas around expressing inner motivation, social isolation, and educational systems that neglect holistic motivational development. Supportive elements encompass inclusive policies, mental health advocacy, and programs promoting social cohesion. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad concludes that the fusion of intrapersonal and interpersonal motivation is essential for balanced human growth. This theory paves the way for individuals to achieve self-realization while fostering meaningful social contributions, ultimately enhancing collective human potential worldwide. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) is an Indonesian scholar, academic leader, and social development advocate with a strong multidisciplinary background. In 2016, YER was awarded the title of Doctor of Humanity, holds a Ph.D. in Information Technology and a DBA in Technology Management. Since 2016, YER has been actively teaching and collaborating with international universities in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and the United States. YER is the founder of the Education Training Centre (ETC, 1992), YER Academic Publishing (YERA, 1993), the Multidisciplinary Academic Institute of Learning (MAIL, 1998), and YER E-Book Publishing (YERE, 1999), institutions dedicated to education, interdisciplinary learning, and ethical academic publishing. His academic contributions have led to his recognition as a Professor and his affiliation with the World Philosophy Foundation. YER is also actively involved in global development initiatives through the United Nations, as a member of the UN Global Compact (id-137635), the UN Global Market (id-709131), and the UN ECOSOC (id-677556). YER has served as a reviewer for several international journals and book chapters, and has written numerous books and articles on a wide range of topics including Philosophy, Economics, Management, Correction for nearsightedness and farsightedness is an important concern for functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) experiments involving visual stimuli in humans. In the absence of personal contact lenses, spherical refractive errors are typically corrected using interchangeable lenses mounted in goggles or glasses frames worn by the participant, or mounted on the head coil during scanning. The coil-mounted device described here avoids the ergonomic challenges encountered with head-mounted goggles and addresses limitations of prior coil-mounted designs, including ease of lens switching and inter-pupillary distance adjustments. Our device can be 3D printed economically with MRI-compatible plastics, including PLA.

Limited work has examined the strategic behaviors of relational networked learning agents under social dilemmas, and has overlooked the intricate social dynamics of complex systems. We address the challenge with Socio-Relational Intrinsic Motivation (SRIM), which endows agents with diverse preferences over sub-graphical social structures in order to study the impact of agents' personal preferences over their sub-graphical relations on their strategic decision-making under sequential social dilemmas. Our results in the Harvest and Cleanup environments demonstrate that preferences over different subgraph structures (degree-, clique-, and critical connection-based) lead to distinct variations in agents' reward gathering and strategic behavior: individual aggressiveness in Harvest and individual contribution effort in Cleanup. Moreover, agents with different subgraphical structural positions consistently exhibit similar strategic behavioral shifts. Our proposed BCI metric captures structural variation within the population, and the relative ordering of BCI across social preferences is consistent in Harvest and Cleanup games for the same topology, suggesting the subgraphical structural impact is robust across environments. These results provide a new lens for examining agents' behavior in social dilemmas and insight for designing effective multi-agent ecosystems composed of heterogeneous social agents.

In a world increasingly shaped by communication and connection, Win Hearts and Minds: Mastering Social Influence with Integrity by Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, offers a profound and ethical roadmap to influence. Unlike conventional approaches that often lean toward manipulation, this book is rooted in authenticity and compassion. It invites readers to understand influence not merely as a tool for persuasion, but as a commitment to shared values, trust, and mutual growth. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, draws from years of academic insight, humanitarian service, and leadership experience to craft a thoughtful journey that reveals how hearts and minds can be reached genuinely—without coercion, and with profound respect for human dignity. Published in 1992 in New York by UNICEF, this work remains a timeless guide for leaders, educators, change-makers, and anyone wishing to create meaningful impact through ethical influence. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA wrote Win Hearts and Minds: Mastering Social Influence with Integrity in 1992, in New York, at a time when the global discourse on leadership was shifting toward emotional intelligence and human-centered development. His motivation stemmed from decades of observing both the power and misuse of influence in societal structures. Recognizing the urgent need for a framework rooted in empathy and ethics, he embarked on this work to redefine influence as a vehicle for collective empowerment rather than personal gain. In this publication, Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA introduces influence as a multidimensional relationship involving perception, trust, and reciprocal communication. Influence, as framed here, is not a manipulation of others’ decisions but an invitation to co-create shared visions. Concepts such as integrity-based leadership, emotional resonance, and cultural alignment are presented as foundational tools for mastering this dynamic. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA wrote this book in response to the rising phenomena of polarized ideologies, public distrust in leadership, and the erosion of social cohesion. He observed that while technology had made communication easier, authentic connection was diminishing. This book became a response to that global condition, promoting influence not as an imposition but as a means of genuine understanding and social alignment. The guiding principle of this book lies in the alignment between internal values and external actions. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA emphasizes the necessity of consistency, clarity, and compassion in every act of influence. The book outlines how social influence becomes effective when it is transparent, participatory, and purpose-driven. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA outlines indicators of successful influence such as increased stakeholder trust, consistent behavioral alignment, and the presence of shared values. The reader is guided to evaluate the depth of their influence not by popularity or obedience, but by the growth and empowerment of those they influence. The book closes with the reminder that authentic influence not only changes others—it transforms the influencer.

The use of AI tools in research is becoming routine, alongside growing consensus that such use should be transparently disclosed. However, AI disclosure statements remain rare and inconsistent, with policies offering limited guidance and authors facing social, cognitive, and emotional barriers when reporting AI use. To explore how structured disclosure shapes what authors report and how they experience disclosure, we present DAISY (Disclosure of AI-uSe in Your Research), a form-based tool for generating AI disclosure statements. DAISY was developed from literature-derived requirements and co-design (N =11), and deployed in a user study with authors (N=31). DAISY-supported disclosures met more completeness criteria, offering clearer breakdowns of AI use across research and writing than unsupported disclosures. Surprisingly, despite concerns about how transparently disclosed AI use might be perceived, the use of DAISY did not reduce author comfort with the disclosure statements. We discuss design implications and a research agenda for AI disclosure as a sociotechnical practice.

documents.abstract: A digital twin is an artificial intelligence (AI)- or human-controlled avatar that replicates a specific person’s identity. While organizations have used digital twins of employees (e.g. digital doctors answering patients’ questions), a more common use is celebrity-as-a-service, where digital twins of celebrities interact with customers. Unlike traditional celebrity endorsements in marketing videos, these digital-twin agents interact directly with consumers. Although digital twins do not enhance the underlying AI or human agents’ capabilities, their appearance as a specific person can influence users’ perception. Across two experiments, we found that when a digital twin resembled a celebrity, regardless of whether it was AI- or human-controlled, it was perceived to be more capable, benevolent, and trustworthy, leading to greater user engagement. Even when errors occurred, the celebrity’s likeness reduced negative reactions, suggesting that celebrity effects can buffer against algorithm aversion. Practically, digital celebrity twins offer business value comparable to traditional celebrity endorsements, influencing user trust and service adoption despite identical underlying performance.

Problem solving plays an essential role in science education, and generative AI (GAI) chatbots have emerged as a promising tool for supporting students' science problem solving. However, general-purpose chatbots (e.g., ChatGPT), which often provide direct, ready-made answers, may lead to students' cognitive offloading. Prior research has rarely focused on custom chatbots for facilitating students' science problem solving, nor has it examined how they differently influence problem-solving processes and performance compared to general-purpose chatbots. To address this gap, we developed a pedagogy-informed custom GAI chatbot grounded in the Socratic questioning method, which supports students by prompting them with guiding questions. This study employed a within-subjects counterbalanced design in which 48 secondary school students used both custom and general-purpose chatbot to complete two science problem-solving tasks. 3297 student-chatbot dialogues were collected and analyzed using Heterogeneous Interaction Network Analysis (HINA). The results showed that: (1) students demonstrated significantly higher interaction intensity and cognitive interaction diversity when using custom chatbot than using general-purpose chatbot; (2) students were more likely to follow custom chatbot's guidance to think and reflect, whereas they tended to request general-purpose chatbot to execute specific commands; and (3) no statistically significant difference was observed in students' problem-solving performance evaluated by solution quality between two chatbot conditions. This study provides novel theoretical insights and empirical evidence that custom chatbots are less likely to induce cognitive offloading and instead foster greater cognitive engagement compared to general-purpose chatbots. This study also offers insights into the design and integration of GAI chatbots in science education.

documents.abstract: Great Minds Grow: Unlocking the Secrets of Intellectual Development is an insightful exploration into how the human mind can evolve and expand its intellectual capacity. Written by Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, and published in 1994 by the United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund in New York, USA, this book presents a compelling case for the idea that intellectual growth is not only possible but essential for navigating an increasingly complex world. The book presents key principles, strategies, and practical exercises designed to help readers cultivate their cognitive potential, foster deep thinking, and unlock the secrets to a more intellectually fulfilling life. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, emphasizes that the mind, like a muscle, requires consistent nurturing and engagement to achieve its fullest potential. This book offers a pathway to personal and intellectual growth, showing that the greatest minds are not born but made through dedication and thoughtful practice. In the 1990s, the rapid advancement of technology and globalization brought new challenges and opportunities for intellectual engagement. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, observed that many individuals were not fully equipped to handle the complex problems and scenarios that emerged in this new era. Inspired by his experiences and research, Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, wrote Great Minds Grow: Unlocking the Secrets of Intellectual Development, published in 1994 by the United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund in New York, USA. The book aims to provide readers with tools to enhance their intellectual abilities and prepare them for the ever-changing world around them. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, believes that intellectual development is a lifelong pursuit that can be cultivated by anyone willing to invest in their cognitive growth. The core concept in Great Minds Grow is intellectual development, defined by Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, as the continual expansion of one's cognitive capacities to process, understand, and apply knowledge. The book presents the idea that intellectual development is a dynamic process, not a fixed state. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, introduces the notion that intellectual growth involves three key components: critical thinking, creativity, and problem-solving. By focusing on these areas, individuals can unlock their potential for deeper understanding, innovation, and meaningful contributions to society. The book provides a framework for enhancing these abilities through structured exercises, reflection, and discipline. The phenomenon that motivated the creation of Great Minds Grow lies in the observation that modern life demands more than just basic knowledge—it requires individuals to adapt, innovate, and solve problems in new ways. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, noted that many individuals were not engaging in activities that could enhance their intellectual capabilities. This lack of intellectual engagement contributed to a stagnation of potential, making it more difficult to cope with the increasingly complex demands of society. The book emphasizes the importance of consistent intellectual development and the cultivation of cognitive skills to thrive in this environment. The principles of intellectual growth outlined in Great Minds Grow are founded on the understanding that intellectual abilities are not static. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, highlights several key principles in the book: • Growth Mindset: The belief that the brain can grow and develop over time through effort and perseverance. • Deliberate Practice: The importance of structured, purposeful engagement in activities that challenge cognitive abilities. • Self-Reflection: The role of introspection in understanding one’s intellectual strengths and weaknesses and guiding personal growth. • Lifelong Learning: The idea that intellectual development is an ongoing process that continues throughout life. These principles guide the exercises and strategies that Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, provides to help readers enhance their intellectual abilities. The indicators of intellectual growth in Great Minds Grow include: • Enhanced Problem-Solving Skills: The ability to approach and resolve challenges with creativity and efficiency. • Critical Thinking: The capacity to analyze, evaluate, and make decisions based on reason and evidence. • Increased Knowledge: The continual acquisition of new information and the ability to apply it effectively. • Creativity: The ability to generate novel ideas and think outside the box. • Self-Awareness: An understanding of one’s intellectual strengths and areas for improvement. These indicators are essential for measuring progress and determining the effectiveness of the intellectual development strategies presented in the book. The operational variables that drive intellectual development include: • Frequency of Intellectual Engagement: The regularity with which individuals engage in activities that challenge and expand their cognitive abilities. • Challenge Level: The difficulty of tasks that encourage growth and the development of intellectual skills. • Diversity of Exercises: The variety of intellectual challenges designed to stimulate different cognitive functions. • Goal-Oriented Practices: The setting of specific intellectual goals that guide and measure progress. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, explains how these variables interact to foster intellectual growth and achievement. Several factors contribute to the development of intellectual abilities: • Intrinsic Motivation: The desire to improve intellectually from within, driven by curiosity and personal interest. • External Support: The availability of resources such as mentors, educational materials, and a conducive environment for learning. • Time and Commitment: The dedication of time and effort to engage in intellectual activities. • Cognitive Flexibility: The ability to adapt to new ideas and perspectives, crucial for intellectual growth. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, offers strategies for implementing intellectual growth practices. These include setting clear goals, regularly engaging in challenging intellectual exercises, seeking feedback from mentors and peers, and creating a supportive learning environment. By integrating these practices into daily life, individuals can foster continuous intellectual development. The main challenges in intellectual development include: • Mental Fatigue: Overextending oneself without proper rest can lead to cognitive burnout. • Lack of Motivation: Without a strong sense of purpose, it can be difficult to stay committed to intellectual growth. • Environmental Factors: A lack of access to resources or support can hinder intellectual progress. • Distractions: The modern world is full of distractions that can derail focus and productivity. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, discusses how to overcome these obstacles by adopting a disciplined approach to intellectual development. In conclusion, Great Minds Grow emphasizes that intellectual growth is a lifelong journey. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, encourages readers to embrace the challenges of intellectual development with determination and perseverance. The key takeaway from the book is that anyone, regardless of background or ability, can enhance their intellectual capacities through intentional practice and a commitment to lifelong learning.

Large language models are changing not only the kind of assistance people receive, but also how that assistance is organized. Instead of working with a single general-purpose chatbot, people can now receive help from systems arranged as peers, specialists, or multiple agents with distinct roles. However, it remains unclear how these forms of plural LLM assistance affect human performance, confidence, and diversity of thought. We conducted two controlled experiments involving 562 participants to examine the effects of using multiple LLMs on mathematical problem-solving and writing. In a math task, participants worked with no LLM, an expert assistant, peer-like agents that surfaced common errors, or both an expert and a peer-like assistant. The expert-plus-peer condition produced the strongest unassisted post-task performance. In a writing task, participants wrote with no LLM, a single generalist assistant, or a pair of role-specialized assistants. LLM assistance improved essay quality, but the role-specialized pair preserved greater idea diversity than the single assistant. Together, these findings identify the arrangement of LLM assistance as a consequential design variable for human-AI collaboration.

documents.abstract: Recent advancements in virtual reality and robotic teleoperation have greatly increased the variety of haptic information that must be conveyed to users. While existing haptic devices typically provide unimodal feedback to enhance situational awareness, a gap remains in their ability to deliver rich, multimodal sensory feedback encompassing force, pressure, and thermal sensations. To address this limitation, we present the Multimodal Feedback Exoskeleton (MFE), a hand exoskeleton designed to deliver hybrid haptic feedback. The MFE features 20 degrees of freedom for capturing hand pose. For force feedback, it employs an active mechanism capable of generating 3.5-8.1 N of pushing and pulling forces at the fingers' resting pose, enabling realistic interaction with deformable objects. The fingertips are equipped with flat actuators based on the electro-osmotic principle, providing pressure and vibration stimuli and achieving up to 2.47 kPa of contact pressure to render tactile sensations. For thermal feedback, the MFE integrates thermoelectric heat pumps capable of rendering temperatures from 10 to 55 degrees Celsius. We validated the MFE by integrating it into a robotic teleoperation system using the X-Arm 6 and Inspire Hand manipulator. In user studies, participants successfully recognized and manipulated deformable objects and differentiated remote objects with varying temperatures. These results demonstrate that the MFE enhances situational awareness, as well as the usability and transparency of robotic teleoperation systems.
